newsitem.title: FINLAND: HELSINKI SUMMIT LOCAL BONANZA, SCANT MACRO IMPACT.
newsitem.headline: HELSINKI SUMMIT LOCAL BONANZA, SCANT MACRO IMPACT.

text.p: Hotels, restaurants and high-street retailers expect a brief bonanza from this week's U.S.-Russia summit, but the event will hardly show up in official macro-economic statistics.
Finland will be squarely in the international spotlight as it hosts on March 20-21 yet another top-level East-West summit; between Presidents Bill Clinton and Boris Yeltsin.

While not expecting much immediate benefit, companies like national airline Finnair and passenger ferry line Silja hope that the army of foreign TV crews, newspaper reporters and photographers invading Helsinki will boost Finland as a destination and yield business in the medium and long-term.
"We believe in the after-effect," Finnair marketing director Leif Lundstrom told Reuters.
"Through television, PR about Finland will reach one billion people all over the world. Finland can become a destination that people take into account when planning their holidays," he said.

Lars Wendelin, managing director of Silja Line, said the summit would raise foreigners' awareness of Finland, "and the better Finland is known ... it will have a positive effect also in our business."

This week, Finnair has extended the business class passenger sections on many European routes expecting more high-paying travellers, Lundstrom said, adding, however, that those revenues "will not alter our financial results."

Wendelin said Silja hoped that some of the summit visitors would arrive by ferry, either from Sweden's Stockholm, Tallinn in Estonia or Travemuende in Germany. "But we don't have any particular summit marketing campaign," he said.

The 2,500-strong media army will lift the occupancy ratio of hotels in the capital region to nearly 100 percent against 58 percent on average in March 1996, said researcher Heikki Lankinen at the hotel and restaurants federation.
The visitors are expected to spend up to 30 million markka on accommodation, meals and other services provided by hotels and restaurants, he said.
"For local entrepreneurs this is a gold mine, but one with a short life-span," he added.
The hotel and restaurant sector would hire up to 5,000 temporary employees for summit-related functions, Lankinen said.

At up-market retailer Stockmann , chief executive Ari Heinio said he expected many summiteers to visit. But even purchases by 3,000 visitors would not affect overall sales much, downtown department store manager Hannu Penttila said.

The steep, but brief, increase in retailing, services and telecommunications will boost these components in the gauge of overall output of goods and services, GDP, and the inflow of foreign currencies will shore up Finland's balance of payments, officials at Statistics Finland (SF) and the central bank said.
"But even if the visitors spend a couple of tens of million markka here it does not mean much for the entire national economy," said an SF official working with monthly GDP data.
"The summit will give a brief boost to the transport and communications component, and to the trade sector," he said.

At the Bank of Finland, head of department Martti Lehtonen said the impact on the balance-of-payments will be negligible even with an upper-range estimate of every visitor exchanging 2,000 markka worth of foreign currencies into markka per day.
"It makes a total sum so small that it will be impossible to later look back at the statistics and pinpoint that, yes, this is when we had the summit here," he said.
The weather is the overriding concern among all businesses, large and small, who expect to benefit over time from the media attention bestowed upon Finland thanks to the summit.
"If the television images being broadcast around the world are filled with sleet, grey and cold -- then we don't have much to gain," said Lankinen at the hotel and restaurants federation.
"If it's sunny and pretty, it will be just great," he said.
According to a fresh weather forecast, Thursday March 20 will offer cloudy weather and snow. On Friday, the weather will be partly cloudy and the sun is likely to come out.
